name: decompose
reasoning: Decomposed into 61 verifiable statement(s). Completeness check passed. Grouped into 5 reasoning segment(s).

statements: The chief concern is a progressively symptomatic skull base/posterior fossa lesion causing lower cranial neuropathies.
The patient has a long history of occipital headaches.
Over the past year, the patient developed worsening speech difficulty.
Over the past year, the patient developed inability to reach high notes when singing.
Over the past year, the patient developed dysphagia.
Over the past year, the patient developed left facial spasms.
Over the past year, the patient developed left hearing loss.
Over the past year, the patient developed tinnitus.
Over the past year, the patient developed dizziness.
These symptoms localize to the left jugular foramen/cerebellopontine angle region.
These symptoms involve multiple cranial nerves.
These symptoms especially involve cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII.
These symptoms also involve cranial nerve VIII.
Salient positive findings strongly support a jugular foramen mass.
Examination showed deficits of cranial nerves VIII through XII on the left.
CT demonstrated a mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass.
CT demonstrated scalloped expansion of the left jugular foramen.
CT demonstrated intracranial extension into the cerebellopontine angle.
CT demonstrated extracranial extension into the carotid space.
MRI showed a 3.8 cm dumbbell-shaped lesion centered at the jugular foramen.
MRI showed a classic “salt & pepper” appearance on T2-weighted imaging.
MRI showed avid enhancement.
The lesion is a highly vascular tumor.
There was mass effect on the left medulla.
There was mass effect on the anterior inferior cerebellum.
There was obscuration of left cranial nerves VII through XII.
There was narrowing of the adjacent left cervical internal carotid artery.
There was nonvisualization of the left internal jugular vein.
This pattern is characteristic of a paraganglioma arising in the jugular foramen region.
There is no description of internal auditory canal-centered disease.
Internal auditory canal-centered disease would favor vestibular schwannoma.
The lesion causes scalloped expansion of the jugular foramen.
The lesion does not cause hyperostosis.
The lesion does not cause a dural tail.
These findings argue against meningioma.
The marked vascular imaging appearance is less typical for schwannoma.
The lesion extends both intracranially and extracranially in a dumbbell configuration through the jugular foramen.
This configuration is classic for glomus jugulare rather than a primary CPA tumor.
Glomus jugulare paraganglioma fits extremely well.
These tumors arise at the jugular foramen.
These tumors are hypervascular.
These tumors show salt-and-pepper MRI signal.
These tumors show avid enhancement.
These tumors show jugular foramen expansion.
These tumors cause lower cranial nerve palsies with tinnitus/hearing symptoms.
Jugular foramen schwannoma is plausible.
Jugular foramen schwannoma can produce a dumbbell-shaped jugular foramen mass.
Jugular foramen schwannoma can produce multiple cranial neuropathies.
Jugular foramen schwannoma can produce CPA extension.
Jugular foramen schwannoma is usually less vascular.
Jugular foramen schwannoma lacks the classic salt-and-pepper appearance.
Meningioma could occur at the skull base.
Meningioma can enhance strongly.
Meningioma more often causes sclerotic bony change.
Meningioma more often causes a dural tail.
These features are less typical than scalloped jugular foramen expansion and prominent vascular flow-void pattern.
Other CPA lesions such as vestibular schwannoma fit the hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness.
Other CPA lesions such as vestibular schwannoma do not explain the jugular foramen expansion as well.
Other CPA lesions such as vestibular schwannoma do not explain the extensive IX-XII deficits as well.

The combination of jugular foramen epicenter, dumbbell morphology with intracranial and extracranial extension, lower cranial nerve deficits, tinnitus/hearing symptoms, avid enhancement, and especially the MRI “salt & pepper” appearance makes glomus jugulare paraganglioma the most likely diagnosis.
Glomus jugulare paraganglioma is the final diagnosis.
